currentContext.strengths: Scale and group backing: world's ninth-largest building materials company, part of the Adani portfolio, with a pan-India footprint across 31 states/UTs|Brand equity: subsidiary ACC recognised 'India's Most Trusted Cement Brand 2025' for the third consecutive year (TRA Research Brand Trust Report 2025)|AI-enabled digital/logistics backbone: CiNOC (Cement Intelligent Network Operations Centre) integrates ERP, IoT, analytics and fleet platforms; 10,000+ IoT sensors; Agnigati digital logistics platform|R&D and product innovation: R&D Centre at Kalamboli driving low-clinker, sustainable-blend material science; premium/performance offerings now 35% of trade sales after the GST cut|Distribution reach: 1,20,000+ channel partners across India (At a Glance) / 60,000+ channel partners and 29,319 contractor partnerships (Human/Social Capital)|Financial strength: highest-tier credit ratings — CRISIL and CARE AAA/Stable (long-term), CRISIL A1+ (short-term); zero gross debt cited in Financial Capital|Logistics integration: modal shift from road to rail, electric/hydrogen trucks, captive ships and jetties reducing cost and emissions
currentContext.strategies: S1 Accelerating Growth: strengthen market position through capacity expansion via both greenfield and brownfield routes, phased to match project pipelines and regional demand.|S2 Strengthening the Iconic Brands: reinforce and maximise the brand values of Ambuja Cements, expanding channel partners, IHB engagement and brand campaigns.|S3 Leading in ESG Standards: reinforce leadership by conducting business responsibly, sustainably and inclusively, and introducing greener products.|S4 Delivering Superior Performance: extract more from the existing portfolio through premiumisation, cost efficiency, volatility management, skill building and digitisation of systems and processes.|'One Cement Platform' consolidation: integrate ACC Limited and Orient Cement Limited into Ambuja Cements (building on the completed Sanghi Industries and Penna Cement mergers) to create a unified, pan-India, globally competitive building-materials entity with simplified corporate structure and stronger operational/financial synergies.|Cost optimisation and disciplined capital allocation to offset input-cost pressure from global energy markets, logistics constraints and currency movements.|Enhance operational efficiency via technology upgrades — modern kiln systems, vertical roller mills, wider Waste-Heat Recovery System adoption, captive power, rail sidings and freight optimisation.|Prioritise sustainability across production, product development and operations — higher blended-cement use, large-scale renewable investments and WHRS deployment.|'Reimaginaction' philosophy: forward-looking agenda centred on agentic AI-embedded operations, decarbonised production and enhanced customer experience, pursued with a calibrated, disciplined approach aligned to market conditions.
currentContext.expansion: Ambuja Cements grew installed cement capacity from 89 MTPA to 109 MTPA during FY 2025-26 through a mix of organic project execution and strategic acquisitions (Sanghi Industries, Penna Cement), and is pursuing a phased, structured path to a targeted 119 MTPA by FY 2026-27, combining greenfield and brownfield additions with low-capex debottlenecking. During FY26 the Company commissioned new grinding capacities at Marwar, Farakka, Sankrail, Sindri and Krishnapatnam, plus additional clinker capacity at Jodhpur and Bhatapara. Projects scheduled for completion in FY 2026-27 (per the AR's project table) are: Salai Banwa Grinding Unit, Uttar Pradesh (2.4 MTPA cement); Dahej Line-2 Grinding Unit, Gujarat (1.2 MTPA cement); Kalamboli Grinding Unit, Maharashtra (1.0 MTPA cement); Bathinda Grinding Unit, Punjab (1.2 MTPA cement); Jodhpur-Penna Integrated Unit, Rajasthan (2.0 MTPA cement; a 3 MTPA clinkering line at Jodhpur already commissioned); Warisaliganj Grinding Unit, Bihar (2.4 MTPA cement); and Maratha Line 2 Clinker Unit, Maharashtra (4.0 MTPA clinker) — aggregating to 4.0 MTPA clinker and 10.2 MTPA cement capacity. The Company has also secured Environmental Clearances (EC) during the year for further expansion at named sites, including: a proposed Cement Grinding Unit at Palwal, Haryana with capacity of 2 x 3 MMTPA (6.0 MMTPA total, EC granted 26.10.2025); a proposed Naulatha Cement Grinding Unit, Panipat, Haryana (EC granted 28.05.2025); expansion of the integrated cement plant at Marwar Mundwa, Rajasthan (EC granted 10.02.2026) together with enhancement of the Marwar Mundwa Limestone Mines ML-I and ML-II; expansion of Cement Grinding Units at Ropar, Punjab and Roorkee, Uttarakhand; and expansion/amendment of several limestone mining leases (Kodidra Block, Kukaras Block, Singsar Limestone Mine and Maldi Mopar Limestone Mine in Gujarat/Chhattisgarh, and the South Boro Hundong Limestone Block in Assam). Manufacturing highlights for FY 2025-26 (standalone) include an installed Waste-Heat Recovery System (WHRS) generation capacity of 133 MW and installed captive power plant capacity of 483 MW.
currentContext.mdna: India's cement demand is expected to grow around 5% in FY 2026-27, following 6.5-7.5% growth in FY 2025-26, supported by sustained momentum in housing and infrastructure.|Demand improved sequentially in H2 FY 2025-26 versus average growth of 6-6.5% in H1 FY 2025-26, with acceleration in construction activity post-monsoon.|A potential further reduction in GST on cement, alongside continued government infrastructure spending, is expected to support demand momentum in FY 2026-27, despite elevated input costs from global supply-chain disruptions.|Per-capita cement consumption in India (~290 kg) remains well below the global average (~540 kg) and ~82% below China, indicating substantial long-term headroom as urbanisation, household formation and formal-housing penetration rise.|Government infrastructure push — the $2.6 trillion National Infrastructure Pipeline, PLI scheme, Smart Cities initiatives, PMAY-G/PMAY-U housing programmes, and China+1-led manufacturing relocation — underpins durable medium-to-long-term cement demand.|Industry-wide capacity additions are projected at 42-44 MTPA in FY 2026-27 (following 50-55 MTPA in FY 2025-26), with capacity utilisation expected to stabilise around 70-71%, stronger in northern/central regions and softer in the south due to capacity overhang (per ICRA).|Input-cost pressures — fuel, logistics, energy, coal, petcoke, freight, and a depreciating Rupee on imported inputs — continue to influence industry margins, reinforcing the need for disciplined execution and cost management.|Premiumisation is a stated margin lever: the GST cut from 28% to 18% has accelerated the shift to premium cement, now 35% of trade sales.|Rural consumption, supported by improving rural incomes and last-mile connectivity, is cited as a counter-cyclical buffer to urban demand fluctuations.|Ambuja Cements' contribution to nation-building is reflected in its involvement in marquee infrastructure projects including the Navi Mumbai International Airport, Chenab Bridge, Atal Setu, Mumbai Coastal Road and World One — cited as evidence of capability to deliver complex, large-scale infrastructure and iconic urban developments (qualitative reference list, not a quantified order book).

risks.risk: Maintaining market position in a dynamic industry environment (R1)
risks.note: Rapid industry consolidation and ongoing capacity additions by competitors are increasing competitive pressure on market share and profitability; mitigated via capacity expansion and brand-equity building through innovation and digitalisation.

risks.risk: Compliance with an evolving regulatory landscape (R2)
risks.note: Regulatory requirements, particularly climate/environmental standards, are evolving rapidly across countries; non-compliance carries reputational and financial consequences, and upgrading strategies to comply can involve substantial cost.

The business is capital-intensive and heavily reliant on energy and resources such as limestone, fly ash and coal, which form a significant share of operating costs, making cost management and efficiency critical to competitiveness.
Ambuja continuously faces potential data leakages that could threaten information systems, requiring ongoing investment in secure environments as digital adoption (including AI tools) expands.

risks.risk: ESG risk — climate, water and biodiversity (R6)
risks.note: Physical climate risks (flooding, drought, heat/water stress) and transition risks (regulatory, technology, market, reputation) may impact operations and supply chains; water stress in certain areas may also affect surrounding communities.
Heavy reliance on limestone and coal makes continuous, cost-effective, quality supply of these resources critical for uninterrupted operations.
Energy costs form a significant share of production costs, particularly in the energy-intensive kilning and grinding processes, exposing the Company to energy-price inflation and supply risk.
Delivering the Company's vision of 119 MTPA capacity by FY 2026-27 depends on timely completion of large-scale projects underway at multiple sites while upholding safety, quality and budget targets.

one-line thesis: Ambuja delivered record annual volume growth of 16% YoY and EBITDA margin expansion to INR887/tonne despite cost headwinds, but Q4 margins were pressured by acquired asset inefficiencies and supply chain shocks; the company is now prioritizing operational stabilization and cost reduction over volume growth, with a clear path to INR150–200/tonne savings from fly ash and green energy by FY27.
financial scorecard: revenue: +12% YoY (driven by volume growth, muted by pricing pressure); EBITDA/margin: INR887/tonne (+12% YoY normalized), Q4 margin compressed by INR250/tonne one-offs (packaging, freight, fuel); PAT (rptd): INR2,647cr (+17% YoY); PAT (normalized): ~INR2,550cr (adjusting for one-off tax reversals and acquisition accounting); order book: not disclosed; net debt: debt-free (net cash position implied by strong cash flow and no leverage)
guidance: revenue growth: 8% YoY to ~80M tonnes in FY27; margin: targeting INR4,000–4,200/tonne cost by FY27E (from INR4,400 in FY26); order inflow: not provided; capex/commissioning: FY27 capex INR6,000–6,500cr; 10M tonnes new capacity (GU + clinker) to be commissioned by FY27 end
segment / subsidiary detail: Trade sales: 74% of volume (up from 68% in Q3); premium cement: 36% of trade sales (up from 35% in FY26); clinker factor: 65% (down from 67% in Q3); acquired assets (Sanghi, Penna): utilization at 57% and 46% respectively; ACC/Orient integration complete (P&L adjustments finalized)
growth verticals / optionality: 10M tonnes new capacity (Maratha clinker, Salai Banwa, Warisaliganj, Mundra, Assam limestone) to be commissioned by FY27; long-term capacity target revised to ~119M tonnes by FY27 (from 155M previously); organic growth prioritized over inorganic; Mundra and Assam represent new geographic expansion
margins & cost dynamics: Q4 cost: INR4,500/tonne (peak); normalized cost: INR4,250/tonne; cost drivers: +INR250/tonne from packaging (West Asia war), freight, higher fuel consumption, branding, lower government incentives; savings expected: INR150–200/tonne from fly ash (railway logistics pending), green energy (32% share in Q4), improved heat efficiency; cost target: INR4,000/tonne by FY27 end
capex / expansion: FY26: INR7,500cr; FY27: INR6,000–6,500cr; focus on optimizing existing assets; new capex directed to Mundra (clinker), Assam (limestone), and high-penetration markets; no major inorganic capex planned
capital allocation: Debt-free status maintained; no dividends mentioned; capital prioritized for operational stabilization, green energy, and disciplined organic expansion; no M&A planned beyond ongoing integrations
risks & watch-items: Soft demand due to inflation/weak monsoon; delayed railway infrastructure for fly ash; prolonged underperformance of acquired assets (Sanghi/Penna); inability to pass on cost increases; geopolitical fuel volatility; GST policy changes
management quality / tone: Confident but cautious; leadership emphasizes execution discipline, cost control, and operational normalization; acknowledges Q4 disappointments but asserts peak cost has been hit; tone is pragmatic, not overly optimistic on near-term pricing
non-obvious takeaways: 1. ACC’s negative operating cash flow is due to intercompany receivables under MSA, not operational weakness — to be resolved via ICD; 2. Premium cement sales (36% of trade) are now the primary margin driver, not volume; 3. Green energy share (32%) is already embedded in cost structure and will compound savings; 4. Naliya railway is not in base model — marine logistics is the real lever for Sanghi

themes.title: Cement demand & pricing recovery
themes.need: Q1FY27 turned cement from a pricing story into a volume-share-plus-fuel-cost story. ULTRACEMCO grew domestic grey volume +13.1% YoY against an estimated ~7-8% industry, delivered its first Rs 5,000cr+ April-June EBITDA (Rs 5,146cr) with EBITDA/ton held above Rs 1,200, and crossed 200.1 MT domestic capacity a year early - but guided Q2FY27 cost UP ~Rs 130-140/ton and pinned the Rs 1,400/ton consolidated target to Q4FY28. The fuel shock, not price, is the swing factor: JKCEMENT's EBITDA/ton fell to Rs 982 from Rs 1,229 YoY despite +19% grey volume, DALBHARAT flagged pet coke 'surged to nearly $160/t' versus a pre-war $110-115, and NUVOCO defended INR 1,079/ton EBITDA only by cutting petcoke from 37% to 27% of fuel mix in a single quarter. Consolidation is visibly compounding (INDIACEM EBITDA/ton Rs 386->400->509->603 across four quarters; DALBHARAT closed Jaypee at Rs 2,850cr EV with Chunar operational and Rewa on trial within 50 days) even as DALBHARAT slipped its 75mt milestone from FY27 to FY28. SHREECEM/RAMCOCEM/JKLAKSHMI/JSWCEMENT/STARCEMENT/BIRLACORPN ride the same volume + consolidation axis.
themes.driver: Q2FY27 is the guided cost trough - ULTRACEMCO ~Rs 130-140/ton, JKCEMENT ~Rs 150/ton and BIRLACORPN Rs 70-80/ton of incremental cost; then fuel-mix agility (NUVOCO's petcoke swing) and whether DALBHARAT's ~Rs 150/t of procurement savings is really 'permanent, not timing'.
